https://www.westerntelegraph.co.uk/news/.text: Entertainment Music Tenby International classical music festival returns to Tenby By Sallie Phillips Reporter Share 0 Comments Tenby International Music Festival returns for its second year next week (Image: Tenby International Music Festival) This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. Classical music will fill the air in a west Wales seaside town this summer as the Tenby International Music Festival returns for its second year. Running from August 13–16, the festival promises four days of concerts and events in Pembrokeshire, featuring international artists from across Europe, North America, and Asia. The programme will include a mix of classical music, family-friendly shows, free performances, and contemporary works. Concerts will be held at St Mary’s Church and Tenby Museum & Art Gallery. The festival will open on Thursday, August 13, at 7.30pm with a collaborative performance featuring the Tenby Male Choir and festival musicians at St Mary’s Church. Founded in 1975, the choir has performed everywhere from local churches to the Royal Albert Hall and is considered one of Pembrokeshire’s most cherished musical groups. Other highlights include an open-air concert in Tenby town centre at 2pm and a children’s concert, Colours of the Coast, at the Tenby Museum & Art Gallery at 5pm the same day. On Friday, August 14, audiences can enjoy Prague to Paris: A Piano Journey Across Europe. The concert will feature works by Mozart, Liszt, Debussy, Mendelssohn, Elgar, and Dvořák. Tenby International Music Festival returns for its second year next week (Image: Tenby International Music Festival) Saturday night’s programme, Fire and Fiddle: An Evening of Hungarian Music, will spotlight the works of Dohnányi, Bartók, Monti, and Brahms. The festival finale on Sunday, August 16, From the World to Wales, will feature traditional Welsh music alongside contemporary works by the festival's composer fellows. New pieces will also be showcased from composer-in-residence Katie Jenkins and composer-in-residence and fellowship director Kian Ravaei. This year’s festival will introduce the Tenby International Composer Fellowship, a tuition-free programme directed by Los Angeles-born composer Kian Ravaei. The scheme attracted 256 applications from more than 30 countries, with just three composers selected: Fiona Frank (Wales), Bea Carr (USA), and Will Stackpole (USA). Their new works will be presented during the festival finale. Featured artists include violinist and artistic director Thomas Mathias (Wales), pianist and co-director Dominic Ciccotti (Wales), pianist Yuki Minami (Japan), and violinist Hana Mizuta-Spencer (England). Also performing are violist Gordon Cervoni (Scotland/France) and cellist Zachary Owen (England). Tickets and more information are available at tenbymusicfestival.com. Photograph: Anna Barclay/Getty Images View image in fullscreen New Zealand’s proposed social media ban for under-16s comes after Australia in December became the world’s first country to impose such a ban. Photograph: Anna Barclay/Getty Images Social media New Zealand to consider banning children under 16 from social media Prime minister Christopher Luxon’s party to introduce bill seeking the ban, citing harm to a generation of children Reuters Mon 24 Aug 2026 01.22 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google New Zealand prime minister Christopher Luxon has said his party will introduce a bill in parliament that ⁠seeks to ban children ⁠under ​16 from using social media, proposing fines of up to 10% of a platform’s global revenue for non-compliance. The bill would ⁠require social media platforms to take reasonable steps to verify users’ ages, including by utilising existing account information, facial technology and ⁠digital identity documents. “We simply cannot accept the harm being done to a generation of ​New Zealand children,” Luxon said ‌in a statement on Monday. “Social media ‌is exposing them to harmful content, addictive technology and pressures they are not ‌equipped to deal with and it’s affecting their family life, mental health, sleep and education.” Four in five under-16s in Australia using social media despite ban, study shows Read more It was not immediately clear if the bill would garner sufficient support to pass through parliament, with one of Luxon’s coalition partners – the New Zealand First party – saying it would not support it. “We have been concerned with ‌the proposed legislation and the direction and slippery slope that legislation like this will inevitably take our country,” New Zealand First’s ​leader, Winston Peters, who is also the country’s foreign minister, said on X. In December, Australia became the world’s first country to ban social media for children under 16, blocking them from platforms including TikTok, Alphabet’s YouTube and Meta’s Instagram ⁠and Facebook. That legislation had been a “colossal failure”, Peters said, adding that ​keeping children off ​social media should be the responsibility ​of parents. “I won’t pretend that it will be simple or ​that it ‌will be perfect,” Luxon ​said at an ​event. “We won’t get every single child off social media. Some will always find ways around it, but frankly, it’s just way too important not to at least try.“ Explore more on these topics Social media New Zealand Christopher Luxon New Zealand politics Asia Pacific news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Australia World AU politics Environment Climate crisis Indigenous Australia Immigration Media Business Health Science Tech Podcasts Newsletters

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/liv.text: A pact between Nigel Farage’s Reform UK and the president of France’s main far-right party on returning migrants who attempt to cross the English channel in small boats has been dismissed by Labour as “a meaningless document packed with daft and dangerous ideas.” Farage sought to hail the Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) as a “landmark” moment. The document includes what Reform described as a “commitment” by Bardella that a National Rally-led French government would accept the return of illegal migrants which have launched from French shores, entered British territorial waters and were returned to France. There are doubts about the practicality of the deal, while in a press conference after he addressed the Reform confernce, Bardella said: “This is more a declaration of intentions rather than commitment.” A Labour party spokesperson, said: Far from being a serious plan, this is a meaningless document packed with daft and dangerous ideas, signed by an increasingly disgraced Reform lead
